Lost in the Slots

Revisiting object-centric representations in the era of foundation models

Priyam Dey* Aditya Sahdev*† Omkar Mahesh Kashyap□ R. Venkatesh Babu

Vision and AI Lab, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore

*Equal contribution. †Work done as a pre-doctoral researcher at the Vision and AI Lab; now at Sarvam AI. □Work done as a research intern at the Vision and AI Lab; now at the University of California, San Diego.

arXiv coming soon Code coming soon BibTeX

TL;DR

Plugged into a foundation VLM, slot-based object-centric representations underperform compared to the dense patch features they are built from, on reasoning, grounding and hallucination benchmarks and at every LLM scale tested. Dense features are not the full answer either: much of the remaining binding failure happens inside the language model.

Abstract

Object-centric representation learning (OCL) has long been proposed as a principled solution to the binding problem, promising improved compositional reasoning and robustness. Yet its effectiveness in the era of foundation models remains unclear. We systematically evaluate whether explicit object-centric (OC) representations improve binding by pairing slot-based representations with pretrained foundation LLMs and evaluating them on diverse open-ended VQA, grounding, and hallucination benchmarks. Contrary to common assumptions, we find that slot-based OC representations consistently underperform dense patch-based features across all settings.

To understand these failures, we analyze slot representations through the lens of the core components of binding, scene segregation and object representation, and identify three key limitations: (i) inferior scene segregation compared to the implicit grouping already present in pretrained visual backbones, (ii) inherent information loss introduced during slot encoding that degrades downstream reasoning, and (iii) weak attribute encoding of fine-grained object properties such as category, color, and spatial position.

Extending our analysis beyond slot representations, we find that although dense visual representations exhibit stronger binding, they are themselves imperfect, with additional binding failures arising in the LLM. Overall, our findings challenge the practical utility of existing OCL methods in foundation models and suggest that future approaches should preserve rich visual information while introducing object-centric mechanisms that enable more reliable multimodal binding.

Three tests, taken from the binding problem

We follow Greff et al.'s decomposition of binding into three functional components and test slot-based representations against dense DINOv1 and DINOv2 patch features on each.

Segregation
Can the representation separate a scene into objects, and at more than one scale?
IsSameObject probe on COCO, §4.1
Representation
Once separated, does each object keep its category, position and other attributes?
Property prediction, reconstruction and RSA, §4.2
Compositional reasoning
Does a foundation LLM reason better over slots than over patches?
Five VLM benchmarks, §3

§3 of the paper

Slots trail dense features almost everywhere

Each vision encoder is connected to a foundation LLM with the standard two-stage LLaVA-1.5 recipe: a projector is aligned on 558K image–text pairs, then projector and LLM are instruction-tuned on the 665K-sample LLaVA mixture. We compare four OC methods (SPOT on DINOv1; DINOSAURv2, FT-DINO and GLASS on DINOv2) against the dense backbones they build on, across Qwen2.5, Phi-4 and Vicuna.

Upgrading the backbone from DINOv1 to DINOv2 lifts dense features substantially. Most of that gain disappears once the features pass through a slot bottleneck.

More slots don't close the gap

Seven slots is the standard setting in the OC literature, so the gap could be a capacity limit. FT-DINO generalizes to more slots than it was trained with, so we evaluate it at 7, 64 and 144 slots (Vicuna-7B).

Performance saturates well below dense DINOv2. Averaging the DINOv2 patches inside each slot's own mask, with no learned slot encoding, does better at every slot count. The loss comes from the slot encoding itself, not from the number of tokens.

§4 of the paper

Why slot representations fall short

Segregation: dense features already group objects, at every scale

We use the IsSameObject probe of Li et al., a quadratic classifier that predicts whether two patches belong to the same object instance, on 500 COCO validation images with at least five objects each. For slot models, two patches count as "same" when they land in the same slot.

Dense DINOv2 wins on medium and small objects against every OC method. The only exception in nine comparisons is FT-DINO on large objects. Dense features encode a continuous spectrum of grouping affinities, so a higher threshold picks out small objects and a lower one captures large regions. Slots fix a single decomposition at training time.

IsSameObject accuracy (%) by object size (Table 9)

Representation: slot encoding throws information away

A linear probe predicts each object's COCO category and normalized position from its representation, with Hungarian matching for slots. Learned FT-DINO slots lose to simple patch-averages over the same masks by 12 points of Top-1 accuracy at 7 slots. Adding slots helps both, but the gap stays.

Against the dense features themselves the gap is larger still: on DINOv2, dense patches beat every slot method on Top-1 and Top-5 category accuracy (figure). The table below isolates the slot encoder by comparing each method's learned slots with a patch-average over its own masks.

The decoder can't bring it back. We take the dense features reconstructed by each slot decoder and test whether they recover what the slots lost. A VLM trained on the original features performs near chance on these reconstructions, so each one gets its own instruction tuning with the same recipe. Reconstructions still trail the original dense features; SPOT on MME is the only exception. The DINOv1 to DINOv2 improvement is not recovered either.

Inside the LLM, slots blur position. Adapting the RSA analysis of Assouel et al. to CV-Bench's 2D spatial questions, we correlate the residual stream at the question-mark token with the queried object's position, layer by layer.

r ≈ 0.25
Dense DINOv2: a sharp peak in layers 21–24, where a spatial index for the object forms
r < 0.13
Every OC method: weaker, partial, and later in the network

Without a clear content-independent positional index, the LLM struggles to bind the question to the right object.

What a good OC method needs: both halves

To separate segmentation quality from representation quality, we keep the masks predicted by DINOSAUR and FT-DINO (FT-DINO segments much better: FG-ARI 48.8 vs 40.5, mBO 36.3 vs 27.7) and swap in patch-averaged frozen DINOv2 features.

With representation held fixed, better masks give better VQA. With masks held fixed, better representations give better VQA. FT-DINO's learned slots waste its segmentation advantage; patch-averaging recovers it. Both segregation and preserved visual information matter.

§5 of the paper

Dense features bind better, but not well enough

If a VLM binds well, objects irrelevant to the question shouldn't matter. We detect the objects a question refers to with OWLv2 and black out everything else. Accuracy goes up on both models and both benchmarks, so distractors do interfere.

To find where, we splice frozen visual tokens: keep the object tokens from the original image and take background tokens from the blacked-out one, or the reverse. Cleaning only the background tokens is enough to recover most of the gain. The encoder is untouched in this test, which places the failure in how the LLM processes the tokens.

A logit-lens view. On a cluttered indoor scene from POPE, the correct token “Remote” barely registers at LLaVA's layer 31 on the original image. With the distractors removed, its probability rises to 0.39 and the final answer flips to correct.

Token dropping as a lightweight fix. Removing task-irrelevant patch tokens before the LLM, rather than blacking out pixels, is a training-free object-centric mechanism. It helps more than blackout on POPE but hurts CV-Bench, most likely because dropping tokens breaks the spatial layout that CV-Bench's relational questions depend on.

The direction this points to: object-centric mechanisms that control which visual information the LLM binds to, designed together with the model, rather than compressing the scene into slots up front.

Takeaways

  • Explicit slots don't buy better binding in foundation VLMs.Across two backbones, three LLM families and five benchmarks, slot-based representations underperform the dense patch features they are built on, and the gap widens as the LLM grows.
  • The slot bottleneck costs segregation and information at once.Slots segment no better than the grouping already implicit in DINOv2, and the slot encoder discards category and position information that a simple patch-average keeps.
  • Binding also fails inside the LLM.Even with strong dense features, task-irrelevant tokens interfere with reasoning. Robust binding needs object-centric mechanisms co-designed across the vision encoder and the language model.
